text.p: Now that he has tucked his record third successive World Matchplay title under his belt, Ernie Els can continue to dream about having another year as good as 1994.
That was when he first showed up at the Matchplay as the player who just four months earlier had won the U.S. Open at the age of 24.

The South African had been the youngest major champion since 1979 and had already won the Dubai Desert Classic by six shots. He went on to win the Sarazen World Open and the Johnnie Walker World Championship.

But he felt that a second place finish that year was every bit as important, when Jose Maria Olazabal in the British PGA nosed him out on the same Wentworth course where he has now achieved his notable treble.
He shot 67 in the final round of the PGA but lost out to Olazabal's 65.
"I really learned how to play the course that week," he said on Sunday after beating Vijay Singh of Fiji 3 and 2 in the Matchplay final.
"I think when you know where to put your tee-ball and whether or not to go for the flag or play safe, it's vital.
"I was 16 under par for four rounds and since then I really know how to play the course. And it suits me, it suits the way I play."
But he conceded: "I did not play as well this week as I did the last two years. My scoring was only about 12 or 13 under par. Last year I was 25 under.
"But the weather was better the past two years, not windy and wet like today."
His triumph boosted him one place in the world rankings to number three, just off his highest rating of two when he won last year.
It seems only a matter of time before he becomes the world's top player and Els feels he is nudging close.
"It comes down to consistency, week in week out," he said. " I was consistent this year for three months, but not the last couple of months."
Remarkably, Els had all but given up hope of winning here on Friday when he fell six holes behind American Steve Stricker in his opening match.
"Nothing had gone my way and I had no confidence," he said. "Maybe I should become a very religious person because I was praying very hard just to reach the last nine."
He won on the final green.
Then he caught U.S. PGA champion Mark Brooks on an off day and won 10 and 8 without playing well.
Brooks rebounded to beat British Open champion Tom Lehman by one hole for third place on Sunday with a 69.
Singh was a tougher proposition after his earlier wins over U.S. Tour moey leader Phil Mickelson and the U.S. and British Open champions, Steve Jones and Lehman.
But four bogeys, one more than in all his three previous matches, cost him dearly gainst Els's greater consistency.
